title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Locksmith and door installation
audience: Locksmith and door installation owners who want more planned work from property managers, real estate offices, strata managers and public bodies in their own service area.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need
Identify public signals that a planned lock or door job is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the planned work you do well, such as rekeys and door-lock upgrades for rental portfolios, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, the job sizes you can sustain, and how often each kind of client needs you. Individual lockouts come from people who need help at a particular moment. This lesson does not target private households, for reasons set out below. A fortnightly round of rental-portfolio work on a route you already run is usually worth more than a single job across town.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column, a status column, a source and a date added. Score each as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit. Ask whether the prospect sits inside your service area, whether it has a repeat need, such as several rental doors or a building's common-area locks, whether you can reach the decision-maker, and whether the work sits inside your licence and insurance. Property managers, real estate offices, strata and body corporate managers, small offices and childcare or aged care facilities are candidates to test. The research did not find evidence of how often these groups buy locksmith work, so treat each as a hypothesis. Use only business contact details published for business use. A business address is not automatically open to marketing.

instruction.heading: Watch public signals
instruction.body: In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders, lets suppliers set alerts, and publishes each agency's annual plan. AusTender does the same for federal work. Council planning permit registers, such as the City of Casey register, show projects at application stage. Use these to decide when to contact a business or public body. Do not use the building permit dataset to contact individual owners or occupiers. The research did not confirm whether that dataset names owners or builders.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message says how you came to know about the need, makes one observation you can verify from a public notice or the business's own material, and offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined set of doors or a fifteen-minute call. The ACCC's July 2026 release on unsolicited selling reported many pressured or misleading approaches, and that about 71 per cent of salespeople identified themselves. An honest, named approach stands out.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide the follow-ups in advance. One reminder after a week and one final message two weeks later, then a pause, is a common pattern. If a prospect says no or asks you to stop, remove them at once and record the date. Review each month which fit tier and which signal produced paid work.

procedure: Write the planned work, area, job-size and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason and a source.
Choose two or three public signals to watch and record the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules and the licence rules for the state before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A locksmith covers three suburbs in Melbourne's south-east. A public tender for door-hardware replacement across several public buildings in one suburb is posted on Buying for Victoria, with a closing date and a named contact for questions. The scenario is illustrative.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the locksmith respond, and what should the response contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The tender is a route the agency has opened, so responding through the stated process is appropriate. Before responding, the locksmith confirms the scope, his capacity and the deadline. He then checks the Victorian licence position with the regulator, because the research did not settle whether a locksmith licence applies, and he does not bid on work he is not authorised to carry out. He does not contact individual staff through private contact details. His response names the tender, says how he found it, offers one defined set of doors with a price basis, and asks one question about access. He does not pressure the agency.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit, status, source and date columns
Written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact, such as a resident's home address after a building notice.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service you are not licensed or insured to deliver in that state.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance for the state before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a locksmith or security equipment service in outreach unless you hold the licence the state where the work is done requires. Victoria's position is unresolved in the research and must be checked with the regulator. New South Wales requires a licence, and Queensland requires a security equipment installer licence. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

A public listing or public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, the OAIC's direct-marketing guidance says public information is not exempt. Whether it applies to your business is not settled in the research. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop when someone objects.

Telemarketing to numbers on the Do Not Call Register is limited to weekdays from 9 am to 8 pm and Saturdays from 9 am to 5 pm, and not on Sundays or public holidays. That is from a 2018 industry guide, so check for updates before calling.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned
summary: Define the planned work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
Any business with a website, because it probably spends money on services
A property group with several sites inside your service area that you already visit

knowledgeChecks.question: A public notice shows planned door works in a building in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Message each resident using their private contact details
Contact the building's manager through a route that the electronic message and Do Not Call rules allow
Go into the common area to look at the work before making contact

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Ask the prospect to like your social media page first
Choose a fun subject line and keep the message short
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending
